card.title: Short Story 1 — The Selfish Giant (Oscar Wilde)

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: ## The story at a glance "The Selfish Giant" by Oscar Wilde is a fairy tale — a short fantasy with a moral — but it is also one of the quietest religious stories in the syllabus. A giant, returning from seven years with the ogre, finds children playing in his garden and builds a wall to keep them out. Spring refuses to enter; the garden stays in winter while the world blooms.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Cause-and-effect chain to memorize: children excluded leads to winter; children admitted leads to spring.
Symbol pairs: wall = ego, winter = selfishness, spring = compassion, rose tree = renewal, little boy = Christ.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: For a 100-word summary use five beats: wall, winter, children return, spring, happiness.  ·  Use exactly the three characters named in the notes - the Giant, the Children and the Little Boy - when a question asks about characters.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Do not add events or characters that are not supported by the notes.  ·  Explain the significance of the wall in the story.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Summarize 'The Selfish Giant' in 100 words.  ·  What is the symbolism of winter and spring in the story?

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Why is the little boy described as a Christ-like figure?  ·  ## The characters worth an essay **The giant** is the story's whole argument: not a villain but a sinner who repents, which is why children and examiners forgive him. Watch the stages — selfishness (the wall), blindness (he blames the weather), insight (he sees the child and the blossom and connects them), action (he tears down the wall), love (he helps the small boy over it), and grace (he is welcomed at the end).…

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## The plot, retold with an eye on its shape The story moves in a clean arc that candidates should be able to draw: **spring without, winter within**. The giant's absence let the children play and the seasons visit; his return and his wall freeze the garden — frost and snow move in, the North Wind rattles the windows, and the flowers will not grow under the stone.…  ·  ## The devices, with evidence - **Symbolism** — the garden is the giant's heart: walled, it winters; opened, it blooms. The seasons are moral states, not weather. The little boy with wounded hands and feet is the Christ figure, and the blossoms that cover the dying giant are the sign of forgiveness given and received.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: For theme questions always name two opposing ideas, such as selfishness versus generosity, not only one.  ·  Answer 'why did winter come?' in one line: because the giant built a wall and kept the children out of his garden.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: How does the giant change throughout the story?  ·  Discuss the theme of redemption in 'The Selfish Giant'.

rows.text: MCQ traps: options saying the giant was always kind, or that the story is only about a garden, are false.  ·  Short-answer areas: the theme of redemption and the symbolism of the garden.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## The themes worth an essay **Selfishness and its cost** — the wall as the story's central image: everything the giant locks in he actually locks out. **Love and sharing as the condition of happiness** — spring enters only where a child is; joy is a shared economy.…  ·  ## How NEB asks it **"Why did the giant build the wall, and what was the result?" (4 marks)** — selfishness, then the garden's winter; the result is the lesson. **"Who was the little child the giant saw last?
